claims.text: Rapid quenching from the homogenization temperature followed by sub-critical annealing will form finely dispersed nanoscale precipitates in magnetic high-entropy alloys.
Finely dispersed nanoscale precipitates enhance magnetic-domain-wall pinning.
Enhanced domain-wall pinning increases the coercive field.
High-temperature homogenization followed by rapid quenching can produce a supersaturated, single-phase high-entropy alloy.
The alloy should be annealed at approximately 0.8 times its melting temperature, within a range of 0.75–0.85 times the melting temperature.
A specifically tuned annealing duration is required.
Processing temperature and cooling rate can alter the phases or microstructure obtained in a multicomponent high-entropy alloy.
The proposed effect requires an alloy composition in which phase separation can be thermally activated.
Nanoscale precipitates form during the proposed sub-critical annealing process.
The nanoscale precipitates act as pinning centers that impede magnetic-domain-wall motion.
The treated alloy will have a significantly higher coercive field than a composition-matched as-quenched sample.
The as-quenched baseline is a supersaturated solid solution without controlled nanoprecipitate formation.
Annealing outside the 0.75–0.85 times melting-temperature range may fail to produce effective nanoprecipitation or may cause undesirable microstructural changes.
The optimal annealing time and the precipitate volume fraction and size distribution needed for maximal domain-wall pinning are not established and may vary with alloy composition.
Electron microscopy and X-ray diffraction can be used to assess precipitate formation and phase constitution in treated and baseline samples.
Failure to observe a statistically significant coercivity increase relative to the as-quenched control would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe the expected nanoscale precipitates would falsify the hypothesis that the specified treatment produces them.
